cards.front: What does it mean that String is immutable?
cards.back: Every method that looks like it modifies a String actually returns a new one
cards.extra: The original is untouched, so it is safe to alias freely: no reference can change what another sees. That is the guarantee behind String's use as a map key.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = "abc";
String t = s.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s + " " + t + " " + (s == t)); // abc ABC false: t is a new String

cards.front: Why can you use + on Strings when Java has no operator overloading?
cards.back: String concatenation is the single built-in exception — it is the only overloaded operator
cards.extra: The compiler converts the other operand to text and joins them. No user-defined overloads exist, in contrast with C++.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = "a" + 1 + true; // the one overloaded operator in Java
System.out.println(s); // a1true
int n = 1 + 2; // on numbers, + is still arithmetic

cards.front: Why is concatenating with += inside a loop expensive?
cards.back: Each pass creates a new String and abandons the old one
cards.extra: Every intermediate result is a full copy waiting to be collected. StringBuilder keeps one growable buffer instead.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { s += "x"; } // each pass creates a new String and abandons the old one
System.out.println(s); // xxx

cards.front: What does StringBuilder give you that String does not?
cards.back: A mutable buffer: append, insert, reverse, then one toString()
cards.extra: One allocation instead of one per concatenation. The book demonstrates the difference by decompiling + with javap.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder("ab");
b.append("c").insert(0, "z").reverse();
System.out.println(b.toString()); // cba: one toString() at the end

cards.back: It returns the formatted String instead of printing it
cards.extra: That makes formatting reusable: build the text once, then log it, show it in a dialog, or put it in a table cell.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String line = String.format("%s=%d", "n", 3);
System.out.println(line); // n=3: format returned it instead of printing it

cards.back: An interface implemented by String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer for read access to characters
cards.extra: A method taking CharSequence accepts any of them. It is the abstraction for "some characters", without promising immutability.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
CharSequence a = "abc";
CharSequence b = new StringBuilder("def");
CharSequence c = new StringBuffer("ghi");
System.out.println("" + a.charAt(0) + b.charAt(0) + c.charAt(0)); // a d g

cards.front: What are the two objects behind regular expressions in Java?
cards.back: Pattern (the compiled expression) and Matcher (a match against one input)
cards.extra: Compile once, match many times. The convenience methods on String (matches, split, replaceAll) hide this for one-off use.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a+");
java.util.regex.Matcher m = p.matcher("caaab");
System.out.println(p.pattern() + " " + m.find() + " " + m.group()); // a+ true aaa

cards.front: What does String.split() take as its argument?
cards.back: A regular expression, not a literal delimiter
cards.extra: Splitting on "|" splits on every character boundary unless you escape it — the classic bug. Use Pattern.quote for literal text.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = "a.b.c";
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(s.split("\\."))); // [a, b, c]
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(s.split("."))); // [] : the dot is a regex metacharacter
